Discussion

Dr. Meadow: Thank you Dr. Roland. I would now like to ask Mrs. Taub to conclude her comments and to discuss the new papers.

Mrs. Taub: Since rage at his significant opponent, as noted earlier by Dr. Adler, is so predominant a feature of the depressed individual, his capacity for intimacy will often be blocked. When anger is experienced, one individual may withdraw, create a physical distance between himself and his opponent, refuse to communicate, and recoil at any attempt to be touched. Another will lash out verbally and/or physically at his opponent, or threaten or even attempt suicide as a means of revenge: “the ultimate punishment” to one's chief opponent. The depressed person may resort to any of these methods of expressing his feelings of rage or he may deny their existence and be genuinely unaware that his depression has anything at all to do with feelings of anger.

The common denominator in all of these reactions is the rage that creates distance between people, foments mistrust, and makes intimacy and open communication unattainable. Impeding the possibility for closeness, trust and open communication are several compelling fears. One great fear is that the extent of their rage will be discovered by others. This possibility generates the fear that any negative feelings expressed by them will subject them to criticism, rejection, and retaliation by others. Another typical concern is over losing control in the process of venting their rage.

When anger at a significant opponent has been neither recognized nor acknowledged by depressed persons, its suppression, or even a dim awareness of the rage, often leads to feelings of guilt, discouragement, worthlessness, low self-esteem, hopelessness, and confirmation of long held feelings of inadequacy.

186

[[RunningHead]]

Existentialism and Psychoanalysis. Charles Hanly. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1979. 298 pp.

Howard Ruttenberg

Howard Ruttenberg

Howard Ruttenberg  

Professor Hanly makes a sustained attempt to refute the theories of Jean-Paul Sartre and incidentally to show the inadequacy of other philosophers' ideas about the human psyche as compared with Freud's ideas. Extended explication of Sartre's ideas is given before they are subjected to criticism.

206

Hanly's outline corresponds roughly to Sartre's Being and Nothingness, but he does not confine himself to that text. He begins with a section on method, before considering the self, relations with others and with the natural world, and concludes with a discussion of the nature of freedom. After Sartre's views are presented, a transition is made by re-casting the phenomenological descriptions into psychoanalytic ones. From the new point of view, Sartre's ideas are seen to be partial and superficial, lacking in perception of the unconscious structures underlying awareness and choice, and of instincts and their conflicts arising out of early relations with significant adults. The form of the argument is a debate in which one side is set up for refutation by the others.

To the extent that Hanly has unified his defense of Freud against philosophy, the debate can be said to be between those who acknowledge the fundamental importance of the instincts and those who do not, for it is not the case with many philosophers, as it is with Sartre, that they equate the psychic with the conscious. What the other philosophers seem to have in common is some idea of the will or reason as free, not subject to the natural law of mechanistic causality. Hanly's task in defending Freud is philosophical. He is concerned with what the human psyche is, how it operates and is to be known and explained, and whether the study of the human being is a part of natural science or a wholly different one based on the uniqueness of human freedom and reason.

These questions were answered by Freud and his followers in the process of developing psychoanalysis as a means of studying human nature and of conceiving of and treating human ills in the light of the understanding derived thereby. The concepts were not developed in sustained dialogue and debate with the conceptions of other philosophers. It is to remedy this omission in some degree, and to thwart the particular challenge from the existentialists that seems to be the motivation for Hanly's polemic.

responseSet.title: Introduction
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Introduction

The papers on Intimacy and Communication which appear in this issue were delivered at the 1980 conference of the National Accreditation Association for Psychoanalysis. They reflect an exchange of ideas between various schools representative of psychoanalytic thought in America today: Adlerian, Drive Theory, Ego, Freudian, Jungian, Modern Psychoanalytic, Object Relations, and Paradigmatic. The conference itself thus dealt, both in process and form, with intimacy and communication.

Because we are interested in the interaction between the participants, we include the dialogues and discussions that took place together with the prepared addresses. Hence the format of this issue alternates formal presentation of papers with informal dialogue. We hope that this approach will convey to our readers the emotional immediacy that was a significant attribute of the conference, an immediacy that is lost when such dialogues are merely summarized in published reports of proceedings. The significance of the events reported here may be better appreciated in the light of the history of psychoanalysis.

Early in its history, the psychoanalytic community responded to differences by fragmenting itself into relatively isolated components, a response reminiscent of the early history of the individual when splitting is a response to differences the immature psychic apparatus cannot tolerate.

115

Editorial Comment

Phyllis Meadow and Hyman Spotnitz

Hyman Spotnitz

Hyman Spotnitz  

With this issue Modern Psychoanalysis initiates a new feature: the publication of clinical material derived from a case of therapeutic analysis. This feature, which will appear from time to time in the future, is introduced herein with Dr. Evelyn Liegner's extensive report on the treatment of a psychotic woman in an outpatient setting. The report is interspersed with passages excerpted from the treatment sessions.

The Journal is privileged to present Liegner's report. One notable aspect of the treatment relationship discussed was the arousal of strong feelings and tendencies to action in the analyst in reaction to the patient's transference. She delineates the patterns of the patient's communications and the use of these induced feelings in her responses. The analyst's “style” as she intervenes to study and resolve pathological patterns of defense is clearly demonstrated.

The appearance of such case presentations in the Journal is prompted primarily by the belief that they provide intellectual stimulation to our readers. To students, in particular, we wish to point out that they are not published to illustrate how patients should be treated or to sanction one or another mode of intervention employed by the writer. In other words, these clinical reports are not presented to guide the student-reader on how to intervene with his/ her own patients. Each report simply constitutes an historical record of what happened between one patient and one analyst in the course of treatment.

Dr. Meadow: It's always a great pleasure to listen to Dr. Kirman describe modern psychoanalytic technique because of the clarity of his thought, and wonderful to hear how he works with patients when they communicate symbolically the negative transference. Thank you, Dr. Kirman. Now Janice Hildebrand will introduce the panel who will discuss this morning's papers and those of Dr. Adler and Dr. Roland this afternoon.

Mrs. Hildebrand: It's a privilege to be able to introduce this distinguished panel who represent the Adlerian, Freudian, Jungian, and modern analytic schools. Mrs. Rena Taub, a training analyst and faculty member at the Alfred Adler Institute of New York, where she is coordinator of the child psychotherapy program. Mrs. Taub is at present engaged in research on depressed women to determine whether there's a correlation between the incidence and severity of depression and sex-role orientation.

Gerald Gargiulo, representing the Freudian school, is a senior member of NPAP, where he's been on the faculty for the past nine years. He's currently an associate editor of Psychoanalytic Review. His special area of interest is the English object relations school of psychoanalysis, and we can expect him to look at these papers today from that perspective, with particular attention to Winnicott. Mr. Gargiulo's papers on psychoanalysis have appeared in the Psychoanalytic Review, American Imago, and Crosscurrents. He is presently writing a text on the psychoanalytic technique from the English object relations point of view.

Dr. Charles Klaif is associate clinical professor at the University of California Medical School in San Francisco. He is also on the faculty of the C. G. Jung Institute of San Francisco. Among his papers are “Empathy and the Analytic Process,” and “The Ego in Analytical Psychology.”

Intimacy as Viewed From a Cross-Cultural Perspective: Aspects of the Self in India and America**

Alan Roland PHD

Alan Roland

26 West 9th Street
New York, NY 10011

Alan Roland   Supervisor, Faculty and Board of Directors, National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis; Research Associate, South Asian Institute, Columbia University; Professional Development Fellowship, American Institute of Indian Studies for Psychoanalytic Research in India, 1977-78. Publications: Editor and Contributor: Psychoanalysis, Creativity, and Literature: A French-American Inquiry; Co-editor and Contributor, Career and Motherhood; Struggles for A New identity; various papers, International Journal of Psychoanalysis and The Psychoanalytic Review.

Francis Hsu, the noted Chinese-American anthropologist, in a 1971 paper, “Psychosocial Homeostasis and Jen: Conceptual Tools for Advancing Psychological Anthropology,”1 admonished his fellow anthropologists for never investigating or defining intimacy relationships in non-Western cultures, particularly Eastern ones. Hsu made the important distinction between the structure and quality of relationships in a society, the former being concerned with the role relationships and structures that social scientists mainly study, while the latter is often involved with the intimacy relationships of a given society that are almost never delved into.

Hsu's formulations struck a most responsive chord when I read his paper a year ago. I had found from some eight months of shortterm psychoanalytic work in India that there is a quality of relationship and relating that seems quite different from what we have here. I thought that perhaps as a psychoanalyst working in the highly intimate therapeutic setting I could make some fresh observations on intimacy relationships in India, and in turn that this could yield a broader perspective on intimacy relationships in our own society.

I recognize, however, that such psychoanalytic formulations would have to take into account differing social and cultural contexts, something which psychoanalysis as a whole has been notably delinquent about.

[[RunningHead]]

Creative Man: Five Essays By Erich Neumann. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1979. Bollingen Series LXI: 2. xvii + 264 pp.

Jonathan Goldberg

Jonathan Goldberg

Jonathan Goldberg  

Eric Neumann, the most distinguished analytical psychologist of his generation and the possessor of a creative gift second only to Jung's, died at the height of his powers in 1960 at the age of fifty-five. The body of work he produced in this relatively short life is of the first importance; at least one major study, The Origins and History of Consciousness, can legitimately take its place at the very highest level of psychoanalytic thought. Thus it has been a most welcome discovery in the last few years that more of Neumann's work had remained untranslated and unpublished in English than had first been imagined. This volume is the most recent posthumous collection.

The major essay in the book is an early one, Neumann's analysis of Kafka's The Trial, begun when he was in his twenties (before he had ever encountered the thought of Jung) and left awaiting revision at his death. Though one familiar with the later Neumann can rather easily intuit the lines of certain changes he might have made in the text, one also recognizes his characteristic mature strengths in evidence: precision of formulation, meticulousness of analysis, depth of concern with the role of creative art, penetrating insight into how the modern psyche meets the problem of transcendance, and awareness of the inter-connectedness of the psychological and the moral dimensions.

The basic problem for modern man, as Neumann interprets Kafka, is that he has lost his relationship to transpersonal reality.

201

Dr. Meadow: I want to thank Dr. Schwartz for helping me to realize the degree to which modern analysis, at least, has incorporated Jungian thought. We need more contact with each other to realize how close our theories have moved. This is a logical result of thinking and working with patients and trying to learn the whole truth about them. [[RunningHead]]

Freud, Biologist of the Mind: Beyond the Psychoanalytic Legend. Frank J. Sulloway. New York: Basic Books, Inc., 1979, 612 pp.

Arnold Bernstein

Arnold Bernstein

Arnold Bernstein  

This extraordinarily exciting and enlightening book should not be missed by students and teachers of psychoanalysis. It is another addition to a growing body of scholarly but iconoclastic literature that is slowly lifting the veil that enshrouds Sigmund Freud and the origins of psychoanalysis in a complex mythology. Freud and his movement, as well as the main body of psychoanalytic theory, are emerging in a new and clearer light, more firmly rooted in the scientific and intellectual currents of the time and relatively free of mystification.

Freud possessed an acute sense of history and his psychoanalytic methodology was essentially historical in nature. He likened psychoanalysis to archaeology. Nevertheless, whether because of or in spite of this, twice in his life (in 1885 and again in 1907) Freud completely destroyed all of his manuscripts, private diaries, notes, and correspondence, thus fostering the Freudian legend and myth of the hero: “I couldn't have matured or died without worrying about who would get hold of those old papers.” A major result of Freud's systematic destruction (repression) of his intellectual past was that, until recently, psychoanalysis appeared to have sprung full-blown from his own head.

It seems to have required an historian (the author of this book is a Harvard-trained historian of science) to undertake the painstaking work of recovering the countless historical artifacts and documentation upon which the book's conclusions rely.

97

The Broken Connection. Robert Jay Lifton. New York: Simon & Schuster, 1979.

Alex Bernstein

Alex Bernstein

Alex Bernstein  

This book is a culmination of Robert Jay Lifton's studies on death. Prior works of his have explored different aspects of death and its effects on society and individuals. This book attempts to synthesize the historical, critical, philosophical, and psychoanalytic views of death into one coherent formulation.

In this reviewer's opinion it is the non-psychoanalytic aspects of the book that stand out. Lifton's thoughtful, insightful analysis of Mishima's suicide, of Japanese attitudes toward death, of the development of the atomic bomb and its effects upon both its creators and its victims left me with the feeling that that must, indeed, have been just what happened.

To Lifton life and death are naturally united, and he asserts that therefore “we must assume that death does not suddenly appear out of nowhere, but is ‘present’ for us in some way at all times.” Of course, he does not mean that death itself is present, but rather the image of death, in the form of “death equivalents” which fall into three classes, “image feelings of separation, disintegration, and stasis.” Each of these is counterbalanced by a corresponding life equivalent: connection, integrity and movement.

In his analysis of Freud's formulations, Lifton states that Freud's error lay in his dualistic view of life and death as opposing forces, although he perceives that Freud had a “unitary vision bootlegged into the death instinct.” In any case, whether these image feelings—which must occur together, in Lifton's view—spring from one source or, as Freud had it, from two, does not affect Lifton's main argument. That is, that it's when the connection between these is broken that problems arise.

The psychoanalytic discussions are less convincing. For example, in considering the case of Ellen West, Lifton essentially accepts Binswanger's exposition, which has long seemed to me to be an elaborate rationalization for allowing his patient to commit suicide while exonerating himself.

This commendable book, both scholarly and well-written, presents an elucidation and a clinical application of the theory of narcissism to the drug dependent/drug abusing personality. The techniques needed to approach and involve drug abusers in the treatment situation are clearly explained. The author competently spells out the modern psychoanalytic reflecting techniques and demonstrates how these techniques are applied through his ample presentation of his case transcripts.

As Adams describes it, the inner mind and the external world of the narcissistic drug dependent personality, is populated by needs, symbols, and a morality that differ greatly from those of the non-drug-dependent narcissistic personality. Herein lies what appears to be a subtle weakness in his thesis.

104

Sex and Eantasy: Patterns of Male and Female Development. Robert May. New York: W. W. Norton & Co., 1980, 226 pp.

Marjorie Sheehy

Marjorie Sheehy

Marjorie Sheehy  

There is no more timely or sensitive an issue than the need for space and a facilitating language in which to discuss what it is that distinguishes men from women. Robert May, a psychotherapist and director of counseling and of mental health services at Amherst

204

College, has compiled well—documented evidence ranging from Greek mythology to the new androgyny on patterns of male and female development. Taking his stand at the psychoanalytic end of the ideological continuum he develops the premise that there are significant psychological differences between the sexes and that what is known as male and female is the result of the interplay of our bodies and our social reality. May takes issue with this statement from Kate Millet's, Sexual Politics: “For the sexes are inherently in everything alike, save reproductive systems, secondary sexual characteristics, orgasmic capacity, and genetic and morphological structure,” as being representative of the position that sex differences are caused exclusively by social conditioning.

In exploring the experiences of maleness and femaleness May reminds us of the archetypal male and female myths of Phaeton and Demeter. The myth of Phaeton who drove the chariot of his father, the sun god, warns of the potential destructiveness of unmodulated pride. The myth of Demeter shows caring confirmed, endurance rewarded, and suffering followed by joy. The characteristics of today's male and female patterns of fantasy are studied through extensive projective testing and the results are reported in detail. The invented stories bear a good deal of similarity to the themes of the Greek myths, and these patterns are found to be evident as early as age six and to peak at adolescence. The underlying pathology of extreme versions of both male and female fantasy patterns is described in two case histories, and the possibility for individual variation and overlap between the sexes on almost every dimension is carefully noted.

The ways in which culture and biology interact in the course of human development are documented with research data from diverse fields of interest. May acknowledges appreciation of Erik Erikson's influence on psychoanalytic thought in the direction of social, cultural and historical factors, and expresses dismay at the distortions of “the complexity, tentativeness, and evolution in Freud's thought” which have led to his being misperceived as the archadvocate of biological determinism. Intimacy and communications on an equal basis with others are alien to the depressives because they fear that communicating as equals will lose them their dominant position, and that intimacy will expose their inadequacy of which they are convinced. They fear they would thus lose their significance and be reduced to nonentities.

As an introduction I want to give you two very pertinent quotations from Alfred Adler, written in 1914 and 1920. He wrote: “The discouraged child who finds that he can tyrannize best with tears will be a cry-baby; and a direct line of development leads from the cry-baby to the adult depressed.”1 “The patient tries to approximate the well-tested picture of a helpless, weak, needy child, for he discovered from personal experience that it possesses a great and compelling force.”2 And: “Tears and Complaints,—methods, which I have called ‘Water-power,’ can be an extremely effective weapon for disturbing cooperation and reducing others to slavery.”3

When we examine the history of a depressed patient and his development, we will nearly always find that he did not recoil from stressing and even exaggerating his weakness, illness, and inadequacy. He has depended since childhood on the active help and assistance from others to an excessive degree. His crying, whining, pouting, his depressed mien, his presenting himself as weak, helpless, and sick, are all means for not only eliciting but even forcing services from others.

An Operational Concept of Intimacy

The subject of this conference, intimacy and communication, lies at the very heart of the analytic experience. If the patient is to learn to communicate effectively and intimately with people in the out-side world, then he must begin to do so in the analytic situation.

Rather than dwell on philosophical and social models of intimacy along the lines of Fromm and Horney, or discuss the juxtaposition of intimacy with isolation as does Erikson, let us rather focus on an operational definition of what constitutes an intimate relationship between patient and analyst.

For our purposes today let us define intimacy for the patient as the experience of feeling emotionally understood by the analyst via the analyst's sharing, withholding or expressing communications to the patient selectively at the right time, in the proper degree. This feeling of being emotionally understood, and thus psychologically loved by the transference object creates in the patient a sense of joy, pleasure, and trust in the analytic relationship. Once this intimacy is experienced by the patient with the emotionally significant analyst, the heretofore perhaps barren world can become fertile ground where close relationships can be cultivated, nurtured, and harvested; a new mode of communication and trust has been established.

When, in Ovid's rendering of the Myth of Narcissus, Narcissus is pursued by the nymph Echo, he flees saying: “Hands off! Embrace me not! May I die before I give you power over me!” This rejection of intimacy is characteristic of Narcissus and of narcissistic character disorders, and it finally leads to his fatal confrontation with his own image in a pool. For another would-be lover, this time a male whom Narcissus had similarly rejected, had prayed to heaven: “So may he himself love, and never gain the thing he loves!” The prayer is heard by the goddess Nemesis, and it is she who is behind Narcissus' infatuation and death.

It is the scene at the pool that I wish to consider and consequently must skip over much of the rest of the myth. But one point should be mentioned in passing, and it will be taken up again in the clinical material I shall present. That is the role of Nemesis and the curse that descends upon Narcissus. A possible rendering of the name Nemesis is envy,1 and it is indeed a curse of envy that torments Narcissus. He is led to desire what he can never have. As we shall see, this underlies his attitude towards the image he sees in the pool and especially causes his inability to relate to the image as the Self, as the center of his psyche. Narcissus can only allow its existence if he can merge with it and possess it.

In centering upon the myth in this way I intend to bring out an aspect of intimacy, especially problematic for the narcissistic character.

Introduction

Since Freud and others saw repeatedly that psychotic patients were incapable of forming the necessary transference attachments, he concluded that any analyst who undertakes to treat such cases “has committed a practical error; he has been responsible for wasted expenditure and has discredited his method of treatment. He cannot fulfill his promise of cure.” Freud's clinical experience had convinced him that psychoses were psychologically irreversible disorders.

Today schizophrenia and psychosis are still considered untreata-ble through psychoanalysis, although more recently a less pessimistic view about the psychoanalytic treatment of these mental disorders has been emerging (Searles, 1965; Arieti, 1954). However, the majority of published clinical reports continue to agree with Freud: it is an impossible task and beyond the therapeutic scope of psychoanalysis.

As contrary evidence, I offer this study of the first four years of treatment of a schizophrenic woman who was helped to become an effective, cooperative, well-functioning analytic patient. This patient proved capable of transference attachments, albeit narcissistic rather than object (oedipal) tranferences.
